item.title: Yes, the Show Has Drawn Raves. But Some of the Objects Are Not Real.
item.description:
A Grover Cleveland campaign kerchief. A Betye Saar assemblage sculpture. A hand-lettered evening gown urging the passage of the long-stalled Equal Rights Amendment (E.R.A.). Posters by Norman Rockwell.

These were among the historical objects featured in the first show in the New York Historical’s new Tang Wing for American Democracy. Built at a steep cost of $175 million, it has been touted as an important expansion for the museum and a capstone to the architect Robert A.M. Stern’s career.

But, just one month since the show opened, none of those objects — several of which were called out in glowing reviews — are on display anymore.

Well, they still appear to be there. But look closely.

The wall labels quietly acknowledge that this object is actually a “reproduction” and that item is a “facsimile.”

This is because it was only as the exhibition — “Democracy Matters” — was about to open on June 18 that the museum fully reckoned with the fact that windows in the new gallery would shower sunshine on some very light-sensitive artworks.

The museum’s first response was to lower blackout shades on the large upper windows. But when Louise Mirrer, the director of the museum (formerly the New-York Historical Society), realized how much that undermined the wing’s soaring architecture, she insisted the shades be raised back up.

“I felt it was disrespectful of the architect’s final museum project,” Mirrer said in an interview. “We had to find a means that could accommodate both the architecture and the exhibition narrative — which we did.”

So, to protect the vulnerable works, the museum replaced 17 of them with reproductions and removed another three.

In one instance, a three-dimensional assemblage by Saar — “Extreme Times Call for Extreme Heroines” — featuring what the wall label describes as a “mammy caricature” with an assault rifle on a washboard topped by a clock — was replaced by a simple digital photograph of the work.

Rocky, Reconsidered: The sculpture is at the center of a show by the Philadelphia Museum of Art that explores the meaning of monuments.

Route 66 Turns 100: Exhibitions recall the history of the neon corridor that helped define the American road trip.

A New Museum Comes With a D.J.: The space in Indianapolis, housed in a former dairy barn, aims to upend expectations of what an art museum can be.

The Fisher Collection in a New Light: A Bay Area family made a deal with SFMOMA that called for exhibitions of the collection’s works every 10 years.

More on Museums: Artists and institutions are adapting to changing times.

In recent days, after The New York Times raised questions about the prevalence of reproductions in the show, the museum said it would remove the photograph because it did not adequately depict Saar’s assemblage.

Much of this has likely gone unnoticed by the many people who have visited and enjoyed the exhibition. The reproductions of Rockwell’s 1943 “Buy War Bonds” posters, for example, which were created by the museum’s digital printer, look strikingly like the images they replaced.

But museums — more so art museums than institutions that chronicle history — have long promoted themselves as places where visitors come in contact with authentic objects. Would patrons wait in long lines at the Louvre to see a reproduction of the “Mona Lisa?”

“What is real? What are visitors’ expectations? Are they evolving with younger generations who are often experiencing things digital first or replicas first?” Devon Akmon, chairman of the board for the American Alliance of Museums, said in an interview. “In a world where we’re seeing more and more things like artificial intelligence, do people want to see what they perceive as being the authentic piece? It’s a really interesting question that a lot of museums and a lot of scholars are trying to determine right now.”

It is certainly true that authenticity matters most in the art market, where the price for a painting thought to have been done by an associate of Rembrandt can soar by millions of dollars when it is re-attributed to the master himself. In such a setting, authenticity is not only a matter of visual aesthetics and visitor expectations, it is the essential foundation of financial value.

Gerhard Schlanzky, a 19-year veteran of the museum who worked on the “Democracy” show before stepping down as the creative director and director of exhibitions last month, was one of several current and former museum staff members who said they were disappointed by the changes.

“You come to see real things,” he said. “Otherwise people might just view them on their devices at home.”

In addition to the Saar, two other items removed from the show were the E.R.A. dress, worn by the Democratic New York congresswoman Carolyn B. Maloney to the 2021 Met Museum gala, and a mannequin in crocheted pink camouflage by the artist Olek that commemorates the 2017 Women’s March on Washington.

Informed by a reporter that their piece had been removed, Olek — who uses they/them pronouns — said in a WhatsApp message from Poland: “Art is safe in storage. But this is not what art is made for.”

Holland Cotter, in his New York Times review of “Democracy Matters,” written when the original works were still on view, cited the new wing’s “primary, high-ceilinged, light-flooded special exhibition gallery,” calling out in particular the Saar piece.

Schlanzky said he recently returned to see the show and was disappointed to find so many objects replaced or removed. “It sucked the life right out of it,” he said. “Particularly upsetting was the Betye Saar piece — to see something so dimensional and bright reduced to this not very good reproduction.”

This was especially distressing, Schlanzky said, given that Saar had just passed away, on July 26.

Alison Saar, one of the artist’s daughters, said in an interview that while she was “a little disappointed,” to hear about the situation, she gave “the museum the benefit of the doubt that this was done with the thought of preserving the artwork.”

“It’s unfortunate,” she said. “But you go down the hallway and can see a huge beautiful show of my mother’s dolls.” (An exhibition celebrating Saar’s 100th birthday featuring examples from the artist’s Black doll collection — a promised gift to the museum — is currently on view in another gallery.)

Schlanzky said Mirrer was aware of the light challenges early on. “The dialogue was always that if we were going to do an exhibition in that space, the windows had to be covered,” he said. “We never would have proposed light-sensitive objects if we knew the shades would be up.”

Mirrer said that, because she had been busy fund-raising for the $175 million project, she hadn’t paid sufficient attention to light issues in advance. She said her priority was to realize Stern’s vision of “a soaring, sweeping space that would invite the city in.”

The show’s curator, Wendy Nalani E. Ikemoto, who left the museum last month, said she had “no involvement in or advance knowledge of” Mirrer’s decision to raise the window shades and replace light-sensitive objects with reproductions. “I have documentation establishing that this decision was made after my departure,” Ikemoto said in an email.

David Nasaw, a historian who has frequently been a speaker at New York Historical, said authenticity is not essential to appreciating and learning from a historical object.

“When we go to Gettysburg battlefield or when we look at the Lincoln Memorial, we can’t see them exactly as the contemporaries saw them,” he said. “Paintings get dirty, buildings decay.

“A reproduction that we know captures the essence of the original artifact — that’s the second best,” he added. “If the only objects we can learn from are the originals, then the historians are lost and the history is lost.”

item.title: He Had Tenure. The New School Laid Him Off Anyway.
item.description:
Professor Sanjay Reddy had been bluntly critical for years about how his university, the New School in New York City, managed its finances. He had thought that his status as a tenured professor of economics would protect him.

It didn’t.

He was laid off in June, along with 18 other New School professors, nine of whom also had tenure. The layoffs are part of an ongoing restructuring at the New School that administrators have said will rescue it from a crisis ignited by shrinking enrollment and crippling deficits. Sixty-eight staff members were also let go. Dozens of additional faculty members have left through buyouts and early retirements, which has shrunk the full-time faculty to 387 professors from 430 a year ago.

The dismissals represent the latest round of turmoil at the downtown Manhattan institution, which was founded as the New School for Social Research in 1919 by progressive professors as an alternative to traditional universities. The New School, which has about 8,500 students, has long struggled with finances, but its latest solution, some professors say, puts its legacy and future as a social science research institution at risk.

The firing of professors amid a larger reorganization has become increasingly common at American universities, particularly since the coronavirus pandemic, said Deepa Das Acevedo, a law professor at Emory University and author of “The War on Tenure.”

Universities, she said, are increasingly acting like other employers, finding “complicated and sometimes pretextual reasons” to fire employees, even those with tenure.

“What we’re seeing at the New School is emblematic of the rising pressures on higher education as a labor market and as an industry,” she said.

The New School’s handling of the layoffs has raised questions among hundreds of prominent professors around the United States and world. They wrote a letter calling on administrators to be more transparent about how the decisions were made.

Professor Reddy’s case is “particularly concerning,” says the letter; Joseph Stiglitz, the Nobel Prize-winning Columbia University economist, is the lead signatory. “The criteria used in selecting faculty and staff for termination have not been adequately explained to the wider academic community,” the letter said.

Professor Reddy, 55, stands out because he was the only economics professor to be terminated. His department is not among the roughly two dozen programs being closed or redesigned. In The New York Times and elsewhere, Professor Reddy had repeatedly been quoted as blaming the university’s financial woes on administrative bloat and bad real estate deals, challenging the official line that the defining problem was a faculty that cost too much.

“I felt, and this was probably naïve and misguided, that I should be able to use tenure in this way,” he said in an interview. “This is what tenure is for. It’s within my professional competence as an economist.”

He was stunned, he said, when he was given two options: step down by July 1 and sign a nondisclosure agreement in exchange for 11 months’ severance, or be terminated, with his last day in December. He chose the latter.

Richard Kessler, the New School’s provost, declined to comment on Professor Reddy’s situation, citing privacy rules. But he said that the university had determined that the economics department, which has nine full-time faculty members, “has more teaching capacity than we have need for.”

He defended the layoff decisions as a whole. “It was a remarkably extensive, and I feel, without any qualifications whatsoever, thoughtful process,” he said.

Paul Kottman, a tenured comparative literature scholar and the chair of the master’s program in liberal studies at the New School, was also terminated. He was asked to continue leading his program until his last day in December. The program, he said, had just received praise in a review process, as did his leadership of it.

The layoffs could set a dangerous precedent, Dr. Kottman said, particularly because they are happening in the center of New York City at an institution known for its commitment to academic freedom. “If my tenured position didn’t protect me, then who does it protect?” he said.

In an interview, Mr. Kessler said that the New School felt it had the right to fire tenured employees, even if their department or program wasn’t ending, because it was reorganizing the entire institution.

Before July 1, the New School consisted of four colleges. Now, Parsons School of Design and the College of Performing Arts have become a single, arts-focused college. A second college merges the New School for Social Research, which is the academic graduate school, and the Eugene Lang College of Liberal Arts, the undergraduate college.

The new structure is designed to reduce costs and increase collaboration, said Mr. Kessler, a musician who was formerly the dean of the performing arts school.

There’s disagreement over whether such a restructuring permits the broad firing of tenured professors. The American Association of University Professors, a nonprofit organization, has shaped the national norms of tenure since 1940. It holds that tenured professors, unless they are being fired for cause, should be let go only in the case of a financial emergency, and only as part of the elimination of their academic program or department.

“A bureaucratic restructuring that leads to the selective elimination of faculty members really puts academic freedom in jeopardy,” said Mark Criley, a senior program officer in the association’s Department of Academic Freedom, Tenure and Governance. It particularly imperils professors “who have displeased administrators or trustees or donors,” he said.

But tenure norms are not laws, and the New School said it was abiding by its faculty handbook, which states that tenured faculty may be let go if there are “serious financial considerations or curricular change(s)” that require the university “to discontinue an academic department/program or college/school.”

Professor Reddy, who has been a faculty member for 17 years, disputed that interpretation. “They’ve used a very innovative and elastic legal theory, a heroic legal theory, you might say, to justify this,” he said.

Nearly all of the terminated faculty members were at the New School for Social Research and at Eugene Lang, because they have had larger enrollment declines than the arts-focused schools, Mr. Kessler said. The university has also paused nearly all Ph.D. admissions, which most affects the social research graduate school.

The History Department is among the most affected: Three professors were laid off, and two are taking early retirement under pressure, said Jeremy Varon, one of the retiring professors. Five professors will remain — “not enough to competently deliver a curriculum,” Professor Varon said.

Mr. Kessler said the cuts reflected that the university had already shifted toward art and design. Between 70 and 80 percent of students are coming to the New School “for some form of design education or creative education,” mostly at Parsons, he said.

Yet most tenured and full-time professors, who are more expensive to the university, work in the social sciences and liberal arts. Parsons, by contrast, relies heavily on part-time adjunct instructors.

“At some point in time, any organization has to take steps to bring the expenses in line with the revenues and also figure out how to plan for the future and essentially invest in strength,” Mr. Kessler said.

Koray Caliskan, a sociologist at Parsons who teaches strategic design and management, saw the restructuring in a positive light. The social sciences, he said, aren’t being lost at Parsons, because they are part of the curriculum for design students. The sweeping redesign of the colleges, he added, could open the way for innovative new doctoral programs.

But Judith Friedlander, a former New School dean and the author of a history of the institution, described the restructuring as a frontal attack on the university’s progressive, social research core.

“It no longer represents what this institution stood for and was about,” she said.

item.title: Questions Mount Over a Star Scholar’s Life and Career
item.description:
For Jason Arday, it has been a breathtaking climb to the top of the ivory tower.

Raised in South London by Ghanaian immigrant parents, Arday says he was diagnosed with autism at age 3, was nonverbal until he was nearly 12 and couldn’t read or write until he was 18. He went on to get his Ph.D. in education, and claims to have had to relearn the contents of his dissertation weeks before defending it after losing his memory following the removal of a benign brain tumor.

In 2023, when he was 37, Arday became the youngest Black professor at the University of Cambridge in its history. That appointment, trumpeted by Cambridge, inspired a spate of glowing media coverage on both sides of the Atlantic highlighting his dramatic life story, including his claims to have once run 30 marathons in 35 days to raise millions of British pounds for charity.

Arday has also told the press that his academic successes brought darker attention, including the delivery of a severed pig’s head to his parents’ home and repeated visits to his office by a masked intruder, once while wielding a knife.

Next week, Simon & Schuster will publish Arday’s memoir, “Great and Unfortunate Things,” under its 37 Ink imprint. In the lead-up to the book’s publication, Arday has found his academic integrity and claims about his biography increasingly under fire.

Concerns about some of Arday’s work had circulated quietly in scholarly circles since the appointment at Cambridge catapulted him to academic celebrity. But they exploded into public view late last month, after a scholar known for racist views about intelligence published a lengthy article in his newsletter questioning parts of Arday’s remarkable personal story and leveling extensive charges of plagiarism against him.

The accusations quickly drew widespread media coverage in Britain, which initially broke down along familiar culture-war lines. To the right-wing media, Arday was a “diversity poster boy.” To supporters, including prominent academics and politicians who signed a petition of support that quickly drew thousands of signatures, he was the victim of a racist smear campaign.

But over the weekend, as questions about his work and personal story continued to mount, a different debate emerged. Is Arday a victim of a campaign to discredit Black scholars? A fabulist whose tales of extreme adversity the academic establishment deemed too good to check? Or both?

So far, Arday’s publisher and university have stuck by him, even as the media has surfaced other questionable assertions — like an apparent claim in a 2022 interview that he had been part of the British documentary series that included the film “Seven Up!,” which began before he was born.

Arday has attempted to clarify or defend many of his claims, including that one. But at times, his responses have added to the controversy.

In an interview with The Times of London published on Friday, Arday appeared to acknowledge some errors in his early work, but blamed them in part on his autism and what he said was insufficient support from academic advisers. And he said he was the victim of a long-running “dark arts” campaign to oust him from Cambridge.

Arday canceled a planned video interview with The New York Times on Monday. But in a statement emailed to The Times by Simon & Schuster, Arday stated that a “detailed investigation” of his doctoral dissertation had “cleared me, acknowledging honest and reasonable errors that did not amount to plagiarism.”

As for his personal life, he said he “had no reason to lie or fabricate,” and reiterated that he was the victim of “a wider campaign, motivated by racism, to discredit me in every single way possible.”

“There is a well-documented playbook for discrediting Black academics in high-profile positions, and it’s been used to devastating effect in the U.S. and now with me in the U.K.,” he said in the statement. “My greatest hope is that what is happening to me now will serve to further expose these actors and forces.”

Simon & Schuster told The Times that it is standing behind “Great and Unfortunate Things,” which it described in a statement as “Arday’s memoir of overcoming remarkable challenges and responding to adversity with resilience.”

“We have worked closely with Professor Jason Arday on ‘Great and Unfortunate Things’ since acquiring it and can speak to the professionalism and integrity he has brought to every stage of the publication,” the statement said. “He worked closely with his co-writer, as well as our editorial and legal teams, to carefully research, write and corroborate the narrative.”

Asked if, at any point in the editing process, revisions were made to Arday’s book to adjust or correct claims that have been challenged publicly, a spokeswoman said that Simon & Schuster does not comment on its editorial processes.

The initial public charges made against Arday last month came from Nathan Cofnas, a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University in Belgium who had previously been disciplined during his time as a fellow at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, following an outcry over a 2024 blog post in which he argued that in a meritocracy, the number of Black professors at Harvard University “would approach zero percent.” (Cambridge concluded in an investigation that his writing did not violate the law or “contravene university regulations designed to uphold free speech.” Cofnas sued Emmanuel College for unlawful viewpoint discrimination, and lost.)

In his newsletter, Cofnas published dozens of excerpts from Arday’s 2015 Ph.D. dissertation that had been flagged by plagiarism detection software, presenting them side by side with passages from a 2009 dissertation by another scholar. The passages from Arday’s dissertation appeared to copy verbatim, or only lightly paraphrase, the other scholar’s work.

Cofnas asserted that Cambridge had tried to cover up and quash criticism of Arday’s academic record and also questioned the veracity of details of Arday’s life story, including his claim to have once run 30 marathons in 35 days.

Retraction Watch, an online publication that covers academic misconduct and research ethics, then weighed in with an article describing criticisms of Arday’s scholarship that scholars began raising privately in 2023. The corrections subsequently appended to some of Arday’s published work, the article claimed, did not fully acknowledge the extent of the changes made.

And over the weekend, British news outlets, including some that previously ran admiring coverage of Arday, raised fresh questions about possible anomalies in his published work and unsupported elements of his personal story, including his claims about the pig’s head and the masked intruder.

Arday’s supporters have said he is a victim of racially motivated attacks. A petition in support of Arday organized by the Good Law Project, a progressive nonprofit, has drawn more than 14,000 signatures, including from prominent figures like Simon Baron-Cohen, who is the director of the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge, and five members of Parliament from the Labour Party.

The petition calls the allegations of plagiarism against Arday “entirely false,” and part of a broader “attempt to undermine Black people who hold positions of influence.”

Asked about the questions surrounding Arday’s academic work, Cambridge’s communications office provided a statement on Monday saying the university takes allegations of plagiarism “extremely seriously,” noting that standard practice is to refer issues to institutions where the research was carried out.

“We have either advised complainants to approach the relevant institution or passed on complaints,” the statement said. “Allegations of plagiarism regarding Professor Arday’s thesis and some of his journal publications have been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University and the journals in question.”

In a statement, Liverpool John Moores University, where Arday earned a Ph.D. in education, said it received allegations of academic misconduct against Arday in September 2025. “A confidential procedure was conducted in response to those allegations and Professor Arday’s Ph.D. still stands,” it said.

But some scholars who have independently examined Arday’s research and citations say they are seeking to uphold academic standards, and that the investigations and corrections so far have not been adequate.

John Preston, an emeritus professor of sociology at the University of Essex who has conducted research on the sociology of education and race, said in an interview he believes there are legitimate flaws that warrant attention and correction.

“The central question of similarities in the text cannot be excused as ‘a right-wing hit job.’ There is a case to answer,” he said. “As academics we have a wider duty to standards, our field of study and the next generation of students. That means admitting if we get it wrong and doing the right thing.”

Martyn Hammersley, an emeritus professor of educational and social research at the Open University in Britain and an expert on research methodology, contacted Cambridge in 2023 with questions about what he said was significant plagiarism in some of Arday’s work. In an interview with The Times last week, he lamented that the political and racially charged debate has overshadowed important questions about academic rigor.

“We now have a public scandal in which right and left confront one another, so that there is not much space for sensible discussion of the issues,” he said.

The allegations against Arday come amid broader concerns about the ways accusations of plagiarism are being weaponized, particularly as widely available plagiarism-detection software makes possible infractions easier to identify.

In late 2023, conservative news outlets highlighted plagiarism allegations against Claudine Gay, the president of Harvard. The university then announced that it had identified several instances of “duplicative language without appropriate attribution” in her scholarly work, which would be corrected.

Gay, a political scientist and Harvard’s first Black president, resigned soon after, calling the campaign against her, which she said was driven in part by “racial animus,” an effort to undermine the university. After Gay’s resignation, one of her chief critics, the conservative activist Christopher Rufo, began highlighting what he said was plagiarism in the scholarly work of several Black women employed by Harvard.

At the time, some observers saw a targeted effort to discredit the work of Black scholars, particularly those whose work focused on race and diversity.

Arday’s work, according to his website, focuses on race, education, neurodiversity and mental health. His 2025 book “We See Things They’ll Never See,” written with Chantelle Jessica Lewis and published by Princeton University Press, challenged “neurotypical hegemony” in the educational system and in society at large.

In a 2023 interview with the BBC, Arday spoke about his first exposures to the rigors of scholarly research as a new graduate student who had only learned to read and write a few years earlier.

“Everything I submitted got violently rejected,” he said. “The peer review process was so cruel, it was almost funny, but I treated it as a learning experience and, perversely, began to enjoy it.”
